screens.title: Memory Consistency in Multiprocessors
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore why memory consistency becomes challenging once you have more than one processor. You will learn the precise problem: multiple processors issue loads and stores concurrently and the system must present a coherent history of those operations. We frame sequential consistency as the simple, intuitive rule that all processors observe the same global order consistent with each processor’s program order. Then we compare that strong guarantee with a set of relaxed models used in real multiprocessors, such as processor consistency, weak ordering, and release consistency. You will see why sequential consistency is expensive: enforcing it needs stalls, flushed buffers, and broad invalidations. To recover performance we’ll learn how fences, acquire and release semantics, and synchronization operations allow programmers to trade explicit ordering for speed. Concrete examples such as a two-thread store/load interleaving and Dekker’s algorithm show how missing fences can cause subtle bugs. By the end you should be able to explain why hardware favors weaker models and what fence placement must guarantee to restore correctness.

keyIdea.title: Core question
keyIdea.text: How do we present a single, consistent order of memory events across processors while keeping performance acceptable?

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Memory Consistency
Memory Consistency in Multiprocessors
Understand the ordering problem that arises when multiple processors read and write shared memory, and learn the models and fences designers use to balance correctness and performance.
In this lesson
What the multiprocessor consistency problem is and why ordering across processors matters.
Coming up
Sequential consistency, relaxed models, fences, and Dekker's example.
Hands-on
A small two-thread experiment that detects weak models and measures fence overhead.
Overview
We will move from a formal consistency statement to practical architectures. You will practice reasoning about what outcomes are allowed under each model and where fences are needed to prevent incorrect interleavings.
Concept Map
Shared memory, visibility, program order, global order, fences, and synchronization form the core vocabulary we'll use. Think of processors as post offices that may delay or reorder letters unless explicit certified delivery is used.
Key takeaway
Strong ordering is simple to reason about but costly. Weaker models require programmer discipline via fences and acquire/release to ensure correctness.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will confidently describe the multiprocessor memory consistency problem and why it differs from the uniprocessor case. You will be able to define sequential consistency precisely, and explain the hardware mechanisms required to enforce it such as stalling pipelines and flushing write buffers. You will also implement reasoning about relaxed models, knowing when processor consistency, weak ordering, or release consistency applies, and you will identify where memory fences must be inserted to guarantee correctness. Finally, you'll analyze the practical performance consequences of these models. For each objective you will be shown concrete examples and a checklist-style metric that verifies competence. This means you will both reason about allowed outcomes for small concurrent examples and design minimal fence placements that restore correctness without unnecessary overhead.

screens.title: How we'll assess understanding
screens.narratorSegment: You will be assessed by explaining why sequential consistency is hard in a multiprocessor and by demonstrating a small experiment that exposes weaker memory models. The hands-on activity asks you to run two threads that perform a store to A then B, and a second thread that reads B then A. You must detect whether the forbidden outcome—seeing B updated but A stale—ever occurs. If it does, that tells you the processor model allowed the reorder. Then you will add memory fences and measure whether the forbidden outcome disappears and how the added fences affect runtime. This shows both correctness reasoning and practical performance trade-offs. The assessment also asks you to reason about acquire and release semantics and to propose minimal fence placements to repair incorrect executions. Being able to argue where a fence is necessary and why a weaker fence suffices is the highest level skill this chapter expects.

keyIdea.title: Assessment focus
keyIdea.text: Detect weak-order outcomes experimentally and justify minimal fence placement while measuring overhead.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Assessment
Guided activity
Run a two-thread experiment to detect weak memory outcomes, then add fences and measure performance impact.
Starter program (conceptual)
/* Thread 1 */
A = 1;
B = 1;

/* Thread 2 */
r1 = B;
r2 = A;
Observe whether r1 == 1 and r2 == 0 occurs. If it does, the architecture allowed a reorder or buffer bypass.
Evaluation checklist
  • Detect the forbidden outcome with many trials.
  • Add fences between writes and re-run.
  • Measure and report runtime differences.
  • Explain why fences fixed the bug and which guarantees they provide.
Why this matters
You will learn to connect formal models to measurable machine behavior and to reason about minimal synchronization for correct programs with acceptable performance.

screens.title: The multiprocessor consistency problem
screens.narratorSegment: The multiprocessor consistency problem asks: when several processors perform loads and stores concurrently, what outcomes should be considered legal? Put plainly, each processor has a program order, but the system must present a single global interleaving of all memory operations that every processor can agree on. A classic tiny example shows the issue. Processor one stores A = 1 then B = 1. Processor two reads B then A. Under sequential consistency certain combinations of read results are forbidden because they would imply that P2 saw the second store without seeing the first in program order. In hardware that uses write buffers or allows memory operations to bypass each other, those forbidden outcomes can appear. The definition you must keep in mind is: sequential consistency requires that the result of any execution is the same as if all operations were executed in some interleaving that preserves each processor's program order. A common misconception is to think each processor can simply use a local write buffer without affecting global order; in a multiprocessor the visibility of buffered stores to other processors determines legality. To check your understanding, imagine two processors swapping stores and loads and ask which read pairs violate program-order preservation. That thought exercise builds intuition about allowed and forbidden outcomes.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Sequential consistency demands a single global interleaving that preserves each processor's program order.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Multiprocessor problem
Statement of the problem
Sequential consistency requires every processor to see memory operations as if there were a single global order that respects each processor's program order. This single-order requirement is what makes multiprocessor consistency nontrivial.
Example
P1: A = 1
P1: B = 1

P2: r1 = B
P2: r2 = A
Under sequential consistency r1=1 and r2=0 is forbidden because it would show B visible but A not, violating P1's program order.
Common misconception
Local buffering is harmless. In fact, buffered stores affect global visibility; other processors may observe buffered stores out of the originating core's program order unless mechanisms prevent it.
Visual reasoning cards
Legal outcome
r1=1 and r2=1 — both writes visible in order.
Also legal
r1=0 and r2=0 — neither write visible yet.
Mixed legal
r1=0 and r2=1 — P1's first store visible but second not.
Forbidden
r1=1 and r2=0 — implies second store visible before first, violating program order.
Key takeaway
When reasoning about correctness, always ask: is there some global interleaving that preserves each processor's program order and explains the observed values?

screens.title: Sequential Consistency: formal requirements
screens.narratorSegment: Sequential consistency (SC) is simple to state but expensive to implement. The rule is: the result of any execution must be the same as if operations of all processors were executed in some sequential order, and the operations of each individual processor appear in this sequence in the order specified by its program. To implement this in hardware requires two concrete properties. First, a processor's memory operations must appear to execute in program order; stores and loads cannot be observed out of order by others. Second, all processors must see the same global interleaving. Practically that implies stalling pipelines when necessary, preventing loads from bypassing earlier stores, and flushing write buffers before later memory operations proceed. I’ll give a tangible pipeline picture: if a store is buffered, the processor must prevent later operations from observing an inconsistent state or must delay issuing later operations until the buffer is drained. The common mistake is to assume per-core order is sufficient; in multiprocessor SC, visibility to others is equally important. For learners, the key check is: could a coherent broadcast of stores to all caches in program order be constructed? If not, SC is violated.

keyIdea.title: SC enforcement
keyIdea.text: SC needs program-order preservation per core and identical global interleaving across all cores — costly to ensure in hardware.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Sequential Consistency
What hardware must provide
Property 1 — Program-order preservation
A processor must not let later operations be observed before earlier operations from that processor.
Property 2 — Single global interleaving
All processors must agree on one interleaving of all memory operations that respects each processor's program order.
Common hardware actions to enforce SC
  • Stall pipelines until previous stores complete.
  • Flush write buffers so stores become globally visible in order.
  • Prevent cache or buffer bypassing by loads that would read out-of-order values.
Process illustration
Imagine a post office queue where each clerk must release letters in sequence and every city receives those letters in the same order. If one clerk holds a letter in a private bag, others may see letters out of order unless the bag is delivered before later letters are sent.
Key takeaway
Preserving per-core order and synchronizing visibility are both required. Hardware that fails either will allow SC violations.

screens.title: Relaxed consistency models
screens.narratorSegment: Because sequential consistency is costly, architects use relaxed models that allow certain reorderings while preserving programmer-visible correctness when synchronization is employed. Processor consistency is close to total store order variants: stores are seen in program order, and loads are seen in program order, but a load may bypass a previous store to a different address. This allows more concurrency without breaking many common patterns. Weak ordering takes a different approach: ordinary loads and stores may be freely reordered, but synchronization operations form ordering points. The programmer is responsible for inserting those synchronization operations to enforce required orderings. Release consistency refines weak ordering by splitting synchronization into acquire and release operations. An acquire ensures that subsequent operations cannot be reordered before it, while a release ensures previous operations complete before it becomes visible. Lazy release consistency further delays propagation of updates until an acquire, minimizing coherence traffic at the cost of more complex update logistics. A common misconception is that relaxed models make programs nondeterministic; rather, they expose reorderings that programmers must control with synchronization so intended invariants hold. Choosing a model depends on the balance between performance needs and the complexity you want to place on the programmer.

keyIdea.title: Relaxed models
keyIdea.text: Weaker models allow reorderings for speed; synchronization or acquire/release semantics restore required order where needed.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Relaxed Models
Relaxed consistency models
Processor Consistency
Stores and loads each preserve per-processor order, but loads can bypass earlier stores to different addresses. Good for many systems where store order matters but independent addresses can proceed.
Weak Ordering
Ordinary loads and stores can be reordered freely. Synchronization ops form ordering points. The programmer must place fences or locks to provide necessary ordering.
Release Consistency
Synchronization is split into acquire and release. Acquire prevents later ops from moving before it; release ensures prior ops complete before it becomes visible.
Example contrast
Dekker’s algorithm needs ordering between a store and a later load. Under weak ordering, without a fence the store may not be visible before the other thread's load, breaking mutual exclusion. Release consistency lets you place an acquire at entry and a release at exit to restore correctness without full fences around every memory op.
Common misconception
Relaxed means random. In fact, relaxations are specific allowed reorderings; correctness depends on using synchronization at the right points.

screens.title: Acquire and release semantics
screens.narratorSegment: Acquire and release semantics let you express ordering only where it matters. Acquire operations are used when taking a lock or entering a critical section. They ensure that following loads and stores cannot be performed until the acquire has completed — you will not observe subsequent operations moving before the lock acquisition. Release operations are used when releasing a lock or performing a synchronization release; they ensure that all previous loads and stores are visible before the release becomes visible to other processors. Together they provide the guarantee needed for lock-based synchronization without requiring a full memory fence for every access. A concrete example: a thread writes shared state, then executes a release when it finishes writing, and another thread performs an acquire before reading the shared state. This pairing ensures the reading thread sees the updates. A frequent mistake is to apply only a release without the matching acquire at the reader; that may leave the reader seeing old values. The important design point is that acquire/release are weaker than a full fence and allow better performance while preserving the correctness of critical sections when used correctly.

Release operations are used when releasing a lock or performing a synchronization release; they ensure that all previous loads and stores are visible before the release becomes visible to other processors. Together they provide the guarantee needed for lock-based synchronization without requiring a full memory fence for every access. keyIdea.title: Acquire/Release
keyIdea.text: Acquires block subsequent ops from moving earlier; releases ensure prior ops complete before the release is visible.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Acquire & Release
Acquire and release explained
Acquire (reader)
Blocks reordering of subsequent operations before the acquire. Use it when entering a critical section so you see the latest updates.
Release (writer)
Ensures all prior operations complete before the release is made visible. Use when leaving a critical section to publish work done inside.
Pairing example: writer updates data then performs a release. Reader performs an acquire then reads data. This sequence guarantees the reader sees the writer’s updates.
Code-like conceptual outline
/* Writer */
data = 42;
release();   // ensure data is visible

/* Reader */
acquire();   // ensure subsequent reads see writer's updates
read = data;
Remember: acquire must be on reader side and release on writer side. Missing either breaks the synchronization guarantee.
Key takeaway
Acquire/release give just enough ordering for lock-based synchronization, improving performance over full fences when used correctly.

screens.title: Memory fences and their types
screens.narratorSegment: Memory fences are the hardware mechanisms programmers and compilers use to enforce ordering. There are several common types: a store fence ensures all previous stores complete before subsequent stores proceed; a load fence ensures prior loads complete before later loads; a full memory fence orders both loads and stores before and after the fence. Acquire and release fences are semantic variants used with synchronization: acquire semantically blocks subsequent operations from being reordered before the fence, while release prevents earlier operations from being observed after it. In practice, fence implementations may differ in cost: a full fence is the heaviest because it blocks operations on both sides, whereas a release fence often requires only that stores be pushed out or visibility be ensured, which can be cheaper. A common error is overusing full fences when an acquire or release would suffice — that increases latency unnecessarily. When placing fences in code, the minimal correct fence is one that restores the program-order visibility required by your synchronization protocol. The hands-on activity helps you feel the cost: add a fence between two stores and measure how much slower a tight loop becomes compared to the unfenced version.

keyIdea.title: Fence taxonomy
keyIdea.text: SFENCE orders stores, LFENCE orders loads, MFENCE orders both, while acquire/release map to synchronization semantics with lower overhead.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Memory Fences
Fence types
SFENCE
Ensures all previous stores are globally visible before subsequent stores proceed.
LFENCE
Ensures earlier loads complete before later loads; useful for ordering reads.
MFENCE
A full fence that orders both loads and stores on both sides of the fence.
Acquire/Release fences
Acquire maps to a fence that prevents subsequent memory operations from moving earlier; release maps to a fence that prevents prior memory operations from moving later. They are typically cheaper than MFENCE when used only for synchronization points.
Example placement: after writing shared state, use a release or SFENCE so the writer's stores are visible. Before reading shared state, use an acquire or LFENCE to ensure later reads see up-to-date values. Over-fencing with MFENCE around every access is correct but will harm performance severely.
Key takeaway
Choose the weakest fence that provides the required ordering at synchronization points to minimize runtime cost.

screens.title: Dekker's algorithm and ordering
screens.narratorSegment: Dekker's algorithm is a classic two-thread mutual exclusion example that directly reveals ordering needs. Each thread sets its flag and then checks the other thread's flag before entering a critical section. Under sequential consistency this algorithm prevents simultaneous entry because each store to a flag is seen in order by the other thread. But on weaker models stores can be reordered with subsequent loads: a thread's store to its own flag might not be visible to the other thread when the other does its check. The result can be both threads passing the check and entering the critical section together, breaking mutual exclusion. The fix is to insert a fence between the store and the subsequent load, or use release on the writer and acquire on the reader. A concrete code sketch shows the pattern: thread sets flag, executes a fence, then reads the other flag. If you omit the fence, the algorithm can fail on processors that allow store-load reorderings. The important misconception to avoid is thinking locks or algorithms proven under SC remain correct automatically under relaxed hardware. Always reason about required memory ordering and add the minimal fences necessary.

keyIdea.title: Dekker's lesson
keyIdea.text: Algorithms correct under SC may fail under relaxed models unless synchronization fences guarantee the necessary ordering.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Dekker's Algorithm
Dekker's example
/* P1 */
flag1 = 1;
if (flag2 == 0) enter_critical();

/* P2 */
flag2 = 1;
if (flag1 == 0) enter_critical();
Under weak ordering, stores to flags can be delayed or bypassed, letting both threads see the other flag as zero and enter simultaneously.
Fenced fix
/* P1 */
flag1 = 1;
fence;              // ensure store is visible
if (flag2 == 0) enter_critical();
The fence forces ordering so the reader cannot observe the writer's store out of sequence. Alternatively, a release on the writer and an acquire on the reader achieve the same effect with potentially lower overhead.
Key takeaway
Prove algorithms under the target memory model or add the minimal synchronization to preserve their invariants under weaker models.

screens.title: Implementing SC: pipeline stalls and write-buffer flushing
screens.narratorSegment: Making a multiprocessor appear sequentially consistent means the hardware must prevent observations that contradict program order and global interleaving. Practically this often requires stalling and flushing. For example, if a store remains in a private write buffer, the processor must prevent later loads from reading values that would imply that the store is visible out of order. One approach is to stall issuing subsequent memory operations until the buffer is drained, or to flush the write buffer to memory or to caches where other processors can see it. Additionally, to ensure all processors agree on the order, stores may need to be broadcast as invalidations to other caches, and confirmation of those invalidations adds latency. The net effect is that every store can cost many cycles while global coherence is established. The misconception to avoid is thinking SC can be provided cheaply with only per-core enforcement; the global agreement requirement is the expensive part. Designers therefore adopt weaker models to avoid stalling on every store and use explicit fences where ordering truly matters. Implementing SC: pipeline stalls and write-buffer flushing means sc requires stalls, buffer flushes, and global invalidations; these actions increase latency and reduce throughput.. In practical terms, why enforcing sequential consistency hurts throughput. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Cost of SC
keyIdea.text: SC requires stalls, buffer flushes, and global invalidations; these actions increase latency and reduce throughput.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › SC Implementation
Hardware actions to enforce SC
Stall pipeline
Prevent issuing later memory ops until previous ones complete, avoiding reorder visibility to other cores.
Flush write buffers
Write buffered stores must be made globally visible before later operations proceed to preserve order.
Coherence traffic and invalidations
Stores often require broadcasting invalidations to other caches. Waiting for acknowledgements yields tens of cycles of latency per store in large systems.
Analogy: requiring every post office to confirm receipt of each letter before the next letter is sent keeps everyone perfectly synchronized but makes delivery slow. Relaxed models let local offices operate faster and only coordinate at lock or fence points.
Key takeaway
The global agreement requirement makes SC expensive; this motivates weaker models and programmer-visible fences.

screens.title: Practical experiment: detect weak models and measure fences
screens.narratorSegment: A concise experiment makes memory models tangible. The test uses two threads and two shared variables. Thread one stores to A then B. Thread two reads B then A. Run this loop many times and count occurrences where thread two sees B updated but A still zero — that outcome is forbidden under sequential consistency. If it occurs, the hardware allowed a reorder or buffer bypass. Next, insert a fence between the two stores in thread one or add an acquire on the reader; rerun many times. If the forbidden outcome disappears, the fence correctly enforced the necessary ordering. Finally, measure timing: run a tight loop with and without fences to estimate overhead. An important practical note is to pin threads to different cores and avoid compiler optimizations that remove memory operations — use proper atomic or volatile primitives in your language so the compiler and C P U do not elide the stores and loads. A common pitfall is interpreting a single run result as proof of model: you need many trials to gain confidence. Conclude by reporting the forbidden-outcome frequency and the relative slowdown caused by fences.

keyIdea.title: Experiment
keyIdea.text: Run many trials of the two-thread test, add fences, and compare forbidden-outcome frequency and runtime overhead to draw conclusions.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Hands-on Experiment
Test sketch
/* Thread 1 */
A = 1;
B = 1;

/* Thread 2 */
r1 = B;
r2 = A;
// record if r1==1 && r2==0
Run millions of iterations and count forbidden outcomes. Then add a fence between A and B and repeat. Use atomic fences or language-level thread fences to prevent compiler/CPU reordering.
Measurement checklist
  • Pin threads to separate cores and disable frequency scaling if possible.
  • Use atomics or explicit fences to control ordering.
  • Measure forbidden outcome count before and after fences.
  • Measure runtime of the loop with and without fences to estimate overhead.
Key takeaway
Experimental evidence connects abstract memory models to real machine behavior and shows the runtime cost of enforcing ordering.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential points to remember. First, the multiprocessor consistency problem arises because multiple processors issue memory operations concurrently and the system must present a single global interleaving that preserves each processor's program order. Second, sequential consistency enforces that global order but is expensive to provide in hardware because it requires stalls, write-buffer flushes, and global invalidations. Third, relaxed models such as processor consistency, weak ordering, and release consistency allow reorderings for performance but require explicit synchronization to ensure correctness. Fourth, fences and acquire/release semantics are the programmer's tools to enforce ordering at synchronization points; choose the minimal fence that preserves the needed ordering to reduce cost. Finally, test small concurrent programs experimentally — for example, the two-thread store/load test and Dekker's algorithm — to observe forbidden outcomes and validate fence placement. Carry these key ideas into your design and code reviews: reason about visibility, not just local order.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Key Concepts
Multiprocessor problem
Ordering of operations across processors determines which outcomes are allowed.
Sequential consistency
A single global interleaving that preserves per-processor program order; expensive to enforce.
Relaxed models & fences
Processor consistency, weak ordering, and release semantics trade some ordering for performance; fences restore necessary order at sync points.
Takeaway

Reason about visibility and program order, use the weakest correct fence, and validate assumptions experimentally.

screens.title: Quick reference: fences and models
screens.narratorSegment: Keep this short reference in mind as you design or debug concurrent code. Store fences serialize stores; load fences serialize loads; full fences serialize both. Acquire synchronizes when you take a lock and prevents later operations from moving earlier; release synchronizes when you release a lock and prevents earlier operations from moving later. Processor consistency enforces per-processor order for loads and stores but permits some cross-address bypassing. Weak ordering lets ordinary operations reorder and relies on synchronization points to restore order. When debugging, reproduce suspect behavior with the two-thread store/load test, then add the minimal fence to fix it. Over-fencing can hide bugs but costs performance; under-fencing leaves subtle correctness errors. This cheat-sheet helps you pick the right fence and the right model reasoning for your performance and correctness needs.

keyIdea.title: Cheat-sheet
keyIdea.text: SFENCE=stores, LFENCE=loads, MFENCE=both; acquire/release pair for locks; test experimentally and prefer minimal fences.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Quick reference
Fences
SFENCE: order stores. LFENCE: order loads. MFENCE: order both directions. Use weakest fence that keeps correctness.
Acquire/Release
Acquire prevents later ops from moving before it; release prevents earlier ops from moving after it. Pair for locks.
Models
SC is simple but costly. Processor consistency and weak/release order give performance with explicit sync points.
Final thought

Always ask: which memory order do I need at synchronization points, and what is the minimal fence that ensures it?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore why memory consistency becomes challenging once you have more than one processor. You will learn the precise problem: multiple processors issue loads and stores concurrently and the system must present a coherent history of those operations. We frame sequential consistency as the simple, intuitive rule that all processors observe the same global order consistent with each processor’s program order. Then we compare that strong guarantee with a set of relaxed models used in real multiprocessors, such as processor consistency, weak ordering, and release consistency. You will see why sequential consistency is expensive: enforcing it needs stalls, flushed buffers, and broad invalidations. To recover performance we’ll learn how fences, acquire and release semantics, and synchronization operations allow programmers to trade explicit ordering for speed. Concrete examples such as a two-thread store/load interleaving and Dekker’s algorithm show how missing fences can cause subtle bugs. By the end you should be able to explain why hardware favors weaker models and what fence placement must guarantee to restore correctness.

By the end of this chapter you will confidently describe the multiprocessor memory consistency problem and why it differs from the uniprocessor case. You will be able to define sequential consistency precisely, and explain the hardware mechanisms required to enforce it such as stalling pipelines and flushing write buffers. You will also implement reasoning about relaxed models, knowing when processor consistency, weak ordering, or release consistency applies, and you will identify where memory fences must be inserted to guarantee correctness. Finally, you'll analyze the practical performance consequences of these models. For each objective you will be shown concrete examples and a checklist-style metric that verifies competence. This means you will both reason about allowed outcomes for small concurrent examples and design minimal fence placements that restore correctness without unnecessary overhead.

You will be assessed by explaining why sequential consistency is hard in a multiprocessor and by demonstrating a small experiment that exposes weaker memory models. The hands-on activity asks you to run two threads that perform a store to A then B, and a second thread that reads B then A. You must detect whether the forbidden outcome—seeing B updated but A stale—ever occurs. If it does, that tells you the processor model allowed the reorder. Then you will add memory fences and measure whether the forbidden outcome disappears and how the added fences affect runtime. This shows both correctness reasoning and practical performance trade-offs. The assessment also asks you to reason about acquire and release semantics and to propose minimal fence placements to repair incorrect executions. Being able to argue where a fence is necessary and why a weaker fence suffices is the highest level skill this chapter expects.

The multiprocessor consistency problem asks: when several processors perform loads and stores concurrently, what outcomes should be considered legal? Put plainly, each processor has a program order, but the system must present a single global interleaving of all memory operations that every processor can agree on. A classic tiny example shows the issue. Processor one stores A = 1 then B = 1. Processor two reads B then A. Under sequential consistency certain combinations of read results are forbidden because they would imply that P2 saw the second store without seeing the first in program order. In hardware that uses write buffers or allows memory operations to bypass each other, those forbidden outcomes can appear. The definition you must keep in mind is: sequential consistency requires that the result of any execution is the same as if all operations were executed in some interleaving that preserves each processor's program order. A common misconception is to think each processor can simply use a local write buffer without affecting global order; in a multiprocessor the visibility of buffered stores to other processors determines legality. To check your understanding, imagine two processors swapping stores and loads and ask which read pairs violate program-order preservation. That thought exercise builds intuition about allowed and forbidden outcomes.

Sequential consistency (SC) is simple to state but expensive to implement. The rule is: the result of any execution must be the same as if operations of all processors were executed in some sequential order, and the operations of each individual processor appear in this sequence in the order specified by its program. To implement this in hardware requires two concrete properties. First, a processor's memory operations must appear to execute in program order; stores and loads cannot be observed out of order by others. Second, all processors must see the same global interleaving. Practically that implies stalling pipelines when necessary, preventing loads from bypassing earlier stores, and flushing write buffers before later memory operations proceed. I’ll give a tangible pipeline picture: if a store is buffered, the processor must prevent later operations from observing an inconsistent state or must delay issuing later operations until the buffer is drained. The common mistake is to assume per-core order is sufficient; in multiprocessor SC, visibility to others is equally important. For learners, the key check is: could a coherent broadcast of stores to all caches in program order be constructed? If not, SC is violated.

Because sequential consistency is costly, architects use relaxed models that allow certain reorderings while preserving programmer-visible correctness when synchronization is employed. Processor consistency is close to total store order variants: stores are seen in program order, and loads are seen in program order, but a load may bypass a previous store to a different address. This allows more concurrency without breaking many common patterns. Weak ordering takes a different approach: ordinary loads and stores may be freely reordered, but synchronization operations form ordering points. The programmer is responsible for inserting those synchronization operations to enforce required orderings. Release consistency refines weak ordering by splitting synchronization into acquire and release operations. An acquire ensures that subsequent operations cannot be reordered before it, while a release ensures previous operations complete before it becomes visible. Lazy release consistency further delays propagation of updates until an acquire, minimizing coherence traffic at the cost of more complex update logistics. A common misconception is that relaxed models make programs nondeterministic; rather, they expose reorderings that programmers must control with synchronization so intended invariants hold. Choosing a model depends on the balance between performance needs and the complexity you want to place on the programmer.

Acquire and release semantics let you express ordering only where it matters. Acquire operations are used when taking a lock or entering a critical section. They ensure that following loads and stores cannot be performed until the acquire has completed — you will not observe subsequent operations moving before the lock acquisition. Release operations are used when releasing a lock or performing a synchronization release; they ensure that all previous loads and stores are visible before the release becomes visible to other processors. Together they provide the guarantee needed for lock-based synchronization without requiring a full memory fence for every access. A concrete example: a thread writes shared state, then executes a release when it finishes writing, and another thread performs an acquire before reading the shared state. This pairing ensures the reading thread sees the updates. A frequent mistake is to apply only a release without the matching acquire at the reader; that may leave the reader seeing old values. The important design point is that acquire/release are weaker than a full fence and allow better performance while preserving the correctness of critical sections when used correctly.

Memory fences are the hardware mechanisms programmers and compilers use to enforce ordering. There are several common types: a store fence ensures all previous stores complete before subsequent stores proceed; a load fence ensures prior loads complete before later loads; a full memory fence orders both loads and stores before and after the fence. Acquire and release fences are semantic variants used with synchronization: acquire semantically blocks subsequent operations from being reordered before the fence, while release prevents earlier operations from being observed after it. In practice, fence implementations may differ in cost: a full fence is the heaviest because it blocks operations on both sides, whereas a release fence often requires only that stores be pushed out or visibility be ensured, which can be cheaper. A common error is overusing full fences when an acquire or release would suffice — that increases latency unnecessarily. When placing fences in code, the minimal correct fence is one that restores the program-order visibility required by your synchronization protocol. The hands-on activity helps you feel the cost: add a fence between two stores and measure how much slower a tight loop becomes compared to the unfenced version.

Dekker's algorithm is a classic two-thread mutual exclusion example that directly reveals ordering needs. Each thread sets its flag and then checks the other thread's flag before entering a critical section. Under sequential consistency this algorithm prevents simultaneous entry because each store to a flag is seen in order by the other thread. But on weaker models stores can be reordered with subsequent loads: a thread's store to its own flag might not be visible to the other thread when the other does its check. The result can be both threads passing the check and entering the critical section together, breaking mutual exclusion. The fix is to insert a fence between the store and the subsequent load, or use release on the writer and acquire on the reader. A concrete code sketch shows the pattern: thread sets flag, executes a fence, then reads the other flag. If you omit the fence, the algorithm can fail on processors that allow store-load reorderings. The important misconception to avoid is thinking locks or algorithms proven under SC remain correct automatically under relaxed hardware. Always reason about required memory ordering and add the minimal fences necessary.

Making a multiprocessor appear sequentially consistent means the hardware must prevent observations that contradict program order and global interleaving. Practically this often requires stalling and flushing. For example, if a store remains in a private write buffer, the processor must prevent later loads from reading values that would imply that the store is visible out of order. One approach is to stall issuing subsequent memory operations until the buffer is drained, or to flush the write buffer to memory or to caches where other processors can see it. Additionally, to ensure all processors agree on the order, stores may need to be broadcast as invalidations to other caches, and confirmation of those invalidations adds latency. The net effect is that every store can cost many cycles while global coherence is established. The misconception to avoid is thinking SC can be provided cheaply with only per-core enforcement; the global agreement requirement is the expensive part. Designers therefore adopt weaker models to avoid stalling on every store and use explicit fences where ordering truly matters. In practical terms, why enforcing sequential consistency hurts throughput. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

First, the multiprocessor consistency problem arises because multiple processors issue memory operations concurrently and the system must present a single global interleaving that preserves each processor's program order. Finally, test small concurrent programs experimentally — for example, the two-thread store/load test and Dekker's algorithm — to observe forbidden outcomes and validate fence placement. Carry these key ideas into your design and code reviews: reason about visibility, not just local order.
